proposed_edges.relationship: Staples history as a disputed Canadian antecedent of environmental history: Cook's continuity claim (1990) and Forkey's rejection (1998)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: In-period texts first; they disagree. (1) Continuity: Ramsay Cook's W. L. Morton Lecture (1990; JCS 25:4, 1990–91) claims a long Canadian concern with environment: 'In a broad sense the writing of Canadian history has always been concerned with the environment' (p. 6). Against reading the older historians as nationalists only, he writes that nationalism 'was not a full-time interest for any of them. Certainly not Harold Innis for whom the fur trade, the cod fisheries and other staple products were the real stuff of history' (p. 6). He also marks a break: 'Innis, Lower and Creighton also struggled with the question of the impact of the North American environment on European women and men', but 'for this earlier generation of historians the exploitation of the environment was accepted as natural and necessary, even though excesses might be deplored' (pp. 6–7), and 'More recent environmental historians have a different focus' (p. 7). (2) Rejection: Neil Forkey (CHR 79:1, 1998) rejects the line: 'Although the environment was an ingredient in the work of Harold A. Innis, Donald Creighton, and Arthur R.M. Lower, their studies do not serve as prototypes for Canadian environmental history'; 'In their approach, the environment exists only as a scaffolding on which human history unfolds, and not as an actor in the process' (p. 70). 'The staples model masks the essential role of social relationships and the dynamic between humans and nature', and 'More appropriate antecedents' are found in the historical geographer Andrew H. Clark (p. 71; n. 6 cites The Fur Trade in Canada and The Cod Fisheries). Classification: 'influence' here records a proposed antecedent that Canadian environmental historians disputed, not an established transmission of method; no in-period text read shows environmental historians taking up staples method, and neither position is presented as the Canadian field's. Later readings (2003–2024), labelled as such and not the evidence this edge rests on: Graeme Wynn (2003 review, p. 96) agrees that Forkey is right 'to puncture' claims 'that the staples approach represents an indigenous form of proto-environmental history'; Wynn (2004, p. 33) writes that the staples works 'focused on human uses of the environment', with 'little concern in this work for the reciprocity and mutuality of relations between people and nature'. Tina Loo (2014, p. 622) reclaims the work: 'it could be argued that some of the most influential work on the country's past was a kind of global environmental history, even if its practitioners did not call it that', naming Innis and Lower. Daniel Macfarlane's entry in NiCHE's 'Crash Course in Canadian Environmental History' (2024) holds that Innis's legacy 'still shapes many key debates and approaches in contemporary Canadian environmental history' and that, through works such as Cronon's Nature's Metropolis, the staples and metropolitan-hinterland theses 'are perhaps Canada's biggest contribution to international environmental history'. The edge records a proposed antecedent the field disagreed over; it does not say that Innis wrote environmental history or founded the field. Innis's books are unread here.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: No environment strand fits. urban_hinterland (Cronon's commodity flows) is the nearest, but the Innis-to-Cronon link rests only on the 2024 NiCHE post and a blog report of an oral remark (2017), both later and secondhand. At release the editor could add a Canadian strand (for example, 'Staples, historical geography and the Canadian field', holding Innis, Clark, Cook, Forkey and Wynn).

edge_111.relationship: Annales geography and multiple time scales as a source of ideas and a temporal affinity for environmental history, acknowledged by Worster (1990) and Cronon (1993); McNeill (2003) later reassessed the Annales treatment of environmental change while crediting their general approach as inspirational
edge_111.evidence_note: In-period acknowledgements first. Donald Worster, 'Transformations of the Earth' (JAH 1990), note 5. Witnesses: the Portuguese translation (Ambiente & Sociedade 5:2/6:1, 2002–03, p. 42, n. 5; PDF read in full) and Internet Archive full-text-search snippets of Worster's 1993 reprint in The Wealth of Nature (ch. 4, n. 5; p. 226 inferred from the running heads on either side; page images not seen; whether the reprint revised the note was not checked). The English JAH page was not reached. Because the English wording is known only from joined search snippets, it is given here as paraphrase: after reporting White's view that frontier and western history had been the formative influence on the field, Worster names French historians and geographers associated with Annales, particularly Braudel, Febvre and Le Roy Ladurie, as a further important source of ideas, distinct from the Turnerian tradition. The translation reads: 'Uma outra fonte de idéias importante, realmente retirada da influência de Frederick Jackson Turner, tem sido a dos historiadores e geógrafos franceses, particularmente Fernand Braudel, Lucien Febvre e Emmanuel Le Roy Ladurie, todos associados à revista dos Annales' (p. 42, n. 5). William Cronon, 'The Uses of Environmental History' (1993; OCR of the author-hosted page scan, journal pagination), p. 14: 'Perhaps this is why we feel some kinship with a Braudelian vision of history in which the different time scales of la longue durée, la vie matérielle, and l'histoire événementielle weave together to form the tapestry of the past. Although our general bias is often toward the longue durée, we understand that the interactions of environment, economy, political institutions, social norms, cultural values, and natural processes are endlessly complex' (n. 29 cites The Mediterranean). Both acknowledge a source of ideas and a kinship, not a lineage, and neither disputes it. Later reading, not evidence for the 1990–93 claim: J. R. McNeill (2003; text-layer PDF, p. 14 re-read) reassesses the Annales treatment of environmental change, writing that 'the Annales historians were, many of them, strangely blind to evolving environments'; Braudel 'normally imagined it as an unchanging force', while Le Roy Ladurie 'embraced environmental change'; 'To a very limited extent, then, Annales historians were engaged in environmental history avant la lettre'; yet 'Their general approach however proved inspirational for many who would become environmental historians'. Gurevich's chapter (publisher abstract only) supports the Annales side: geography among the school's concerns; it says nothing about environmental history. Earlier wording (an undirected comparison of affinities) is replaced because Worster and Cronon describe influence running from the Annales to the field, not a comparison between equals.

Later reading: Loo (2014) reclaims the work as 'a kind of global environmental history'. Books unread here.
